'''Jean-Pierre Leburton''' (March 4, 1949, [[Liège]], [[Belgium]])<ref name="Kalte">{{cite book |last1=Kalte |first1=Pamela M. |title=American men & women of science |last2=Nemeh |first2=Katherine H. |date=2003 |publisher=Gale |isbn=978-0-7876-6523-4 |edition=21 |volume=4 |location=Detroit |page=690}}</ref> is a physicist and engineer who is the Gregory E. Stillman Emeritus Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the [[University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign]].<ref name="Illinois">{{cite web|title=Jean-Pierre Leburton Professor of Electrical and Computer Eng.|url=https://physics.illinois.edu/people/directory/profile/jleburto|website=Physics Illinois|access-date=18 December 2017}}</ref>

Leburton is also a Research Professor in the N. Holonyak Jr Micro and Technology Laboratory.<ref name="Waremme">{{cite web |title=Chronique de Waremme |url=http://www.chronique-waremme.be/tag/charlotte-joniaux/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180128021252/http://www.chronique-waremme.be/tag/charlotte-joniaux/ |archive-date=28 January 2018 |access-date=19 December 2017 |website=Waremme}}</ref> He is known for his work on the theory and simulation of [[semiconductors]], and quantum devices including [[quantum wires]], [[quantum dots]], and [[quantum well]]s.<ref name="Waremme" /> He studies and develops physical models for [[Nanotechnology|nanoscale]] materials and devices with potential applications in electronics, [[photonics]], biology and medicine.<ref name="McGaughey" />

==Early life and education==
Leburton was born in [[Liège|Liège, Belgium]],<ref name="Waremme"/> to [[Edmond Leburton]], a Belgian statesman and former Prime Minister, and Charlotte Joniaux.<ref name="McGaughey">{{cite news|last1=McGaughey|first1=Steve|title=Father's Gift Led Leburton to Science|url=https://beckman.illinois.edu/news/2007/08/082207|access-date=19 December 2017|work=Beckman Institute|date=August 22, 2007}}</ref> His grandfather, Charles Joniaux, was a [[civil engineer]] involved in the construction of the Peking–Hankow railroad in China in the early 20th century. Leburton had one younger brother, Eddy Leburton, who died in 1993.<ref name=":0">https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?arnumber=9546710

Perspectives in Quantum Devices and Computational Nanotechnology by Jean-Pierre Leburton</ref>

Leburton attended the Athénée Adolf Max in Brussels and later completed his secondary education at the Athénée Royal in [[Waregem|Waremme, Belgium]]. He earned a licentiate degree in physics from the [[University of Liège]] in 1971, graduating ''magna cum laude''. After two years as a teaching assistant and a year of teaching in Morocco, he returned to Liège and completed a Ph.D. in theoretical physics in 1978 with ''[[summa cum laude]]'' honors.<ref name=":0" />

==Career==
Leburton began his professional career in 1979 as a research scientist at the Siemens AG Research Laboratory in [[Munich, West Germany]], where he worked until 1981.<ref name="Woo" /><ref name="Kalte" /><ref name="SPIE">{{cite journal |last1=Leburton |first1=Jean-Pierre |date=3 November 2015 |title=Genomics with graphene nanotechnology |url=http://spie.org/newsroom/6115-genomics-with-graphene-nanotechnology?SSO=1 |journal=SPIE Newsroom |doi=10.1117/2.1201510.006115 |url-access=subscription |access-date=19 December 2017}}</ref> In that year, he moved to the United States to join the [[University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign]] (UIUC) as a visiting assistant professor until 1983 when he joined the Faculty as an assistant professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering.

He was promoted to associate professor in 1987 and to full professor in 1991. During this period, he collaborated with [[Karl Hess (scientist)|Karl Hess]], a prominent figure in [[semiconductor device]] theory and co-director of the newly established Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology.<ref name="McGaughey" /> In 2003, he was named the Gregory E. Stillman Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, a chaired position he held until 2023.<ref name="Illinois" />

In 1989, Leburton became one of the original faculty members at the [[Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology|Beckman Institute]], contributing to its interdisciplinary mission from its inception to 2018.<ref name="IOP" /> His research evolved from traditional [[semiconductor physics]] involving low-dimensional electronic and photonic devices such as quantum wires and quantum dots to pioneering work in the integration of nanoscale semiconductors with biological systems.<ref name="IEEE">{{cite news |date=2017 |title=Leburton Honored by IEEE |url=https://beckman.illinois.edu/news/publications/bulletin/bulletin-2017-january |access-date=21 December 2017 |work=Beckman Bulletin |issue=January}}</ref>

Leburton was among the early advocates for applying nanoscale solid-state devices to bio-molecular sensing.<ref name="IOP" /> He proposed and developed semiconductor nanopore technologies for DNA sequencing and biosensing applications, leveraging solid-state membranes to improve electrical sensitivity.<ref name="IOP" />

In addition to his primary faculty role, Leburton held several visiting positions abroad. In 1992, he was appointed to the Hitachi Ltd. Chair on Quantum Materials as a visiting professor at the [[University of Tokyo|University of Tokyo in Japan]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Iliyah |date=2021-04-07 |title=  Small but Mighty: Game-Changing Nanopore Research|url=https://www.scientia.global/dr-jean-pierre-leburton-small-but-mighty-game-changing-nanopore-research/ |journal= Scientia|language=en-US |doi=10.33548/SCIENTIA654|doi-access=free }}</ref> Later, in 2000, he served as a visiting professor at the [[Swiss Federal Institute of Technology]] in [[Lausanne]] (EPFL), further expanding his international academic collaborations.<ref name="Conference2017">{{cite web |title=2nd World Biotechnology Congress December 04-05, 2017 |url=https://world.biotechnologycongress.com/ocm/2017/jean-pierre-leburton-university-of-illinois-usa |access-date=21 December 2017 |website=Conference Series |date=14 September 2017 }}</ref>

That year, in recognition of his longstanding service and accomplishments, he was named Gregory Stillman Emeritus Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering. From 2008 to 2023, he also held a joint appointment as Professor of Physics at the University of Illinois, reflecting the interdisciplinary scope of his work.<ref name="Illinois" /> Since 2011, he has concurrently served as an adjunct professor at the [[University of Illinois Chicago|University of Illinois at Chicago.]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2020-11-24 |title=Jean-Pierre Leburton, winner of the 2021 "Pioneer award" from the Nanotechnology Council |url=https://www.uliege.be/cms/c_12940264/en/jean-pierre-leburton-winner-of-the-2021-pioneer-award-from-the-nanotechnology-council |access-date=2025-09-03 |website=www.uliege.be |language=en}}</ref>

In 2004, he received the Quantum Device Award from the International Symposium on Compound Semiconductors for his contributions to nanoscale device physics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Quantum Devices Award |url=https://www.csw2018.org/new-page-1 |access-date=2025-09-03 |website=Compound Semiconductor Week 2018 |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2011, he was elected to the [[Royal Academies for Science and the Arts of Belgium|Royal Academy of Sciences]], Letters and Fine Arts of Belgium.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Leburton named associate member of Royal Academy of Belgium |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/729474 |access-date=2025-09-03 |website=EurekAlert! |language=en}}</ref>

He has also been honored with the Gold Medal for Scientific Achievement by the alumni association of the [[University of Liège]] and was named a Chevalier dans l'Ordre des Palmes Académiques by the French government in recognition of his scientific and academic contributions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Distinguished Lecturers |url=https://ieeenano.org/educational-activities/distinguished-lecturers/ |access-date=2025-09-03 |website=IEEE Nanotechnology Council |language=en-US}}</ref>

More recently in 2021, he was selected for the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers|IEEE]] Nano Technology Council Pioneer Award for his pioneered contribution to the modeling and simulation of semiconductor [[nanostructure]] and quantum devices.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="IEEE" />

Over the course of his career, Leburton has authored and coauthored over 400 scientific publications in technical journals, books and conference proceedings and delivered more than 350 presentations as plenary addresses, keynote and invited talks at conferences and research institutions, worldwide.<ref name="Conference2017" />

He has chaired international conferences, such as the International Conference on Superlattices, Nanostructures and Nanodevices (ICSNN), and played a significant leadership role in the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers|IEEE Nanotechnology Council]]. His editorial work includes being the editor of ''Phonons in Semiconductor Nanostructures'' (1993)<ref name="Pascual">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iHLoCAAAQBAJ&q=Leburton |title=Phonons in semiconductor nanostructures |date=1993 |publisher=Kluwer Academic |isbn=978-0-7923-2277-1 |editor-last1=Leburton |editor-first1=Jean-Pierre |location=Dordrecht |editor-last2=Pascual |editor-first2=Jordi |editor-last3=Torres |editor-first3=Clivia Sotomayor |access-date=27 December 2017}}</ref> and co-editor of ''Contemporary Topics in Semiconductor Spintronics'' (2017), among others.<ref name="Bandyopadhyay">{{cite book |last1=Bandyopadhyay |first1=Supriyo |title=Contemporary Topics in Semiconductor Spintronics |last2=Cahay |first2=Marc |last3=Leburton |first3=Jean-Pierre |date=2017 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-314-981-6 |doi=10.1142/10273}}</ref> More recently, he edited a book on ''Physical Model for Quantum Dots.''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Physical Models for Quantum Dots |url=https://www.jennystanford.com/9781003148494/physical-models-for-quantum-dots/ |access-date=2025-09-03 |website=Jenny Stanford Publishing |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Research==
Leburton's research career spans over four decades and has influenced [[nanoscale]] [[semiconductor physics]], quantum device theory, [[spintronics]], and bio-nanoelectronics.<ref name="Moone"/> Renowned for integrating fundamental [[solid-state physics]] with advanced computational techniques, his work has shaped emerging technologies in optoelectronics, memory devices, biosensors, and quantum computing.<ref name="Russell">{{cite news|last1=Russell|first1=John|title=Promising Spintronic Switch Proposed by UTD Researcher-led Team|url=https://www.hpcwire.com/2017/06/08/promising-spintronic-switch-proposed-utd-researcher-led-team/|access-date=28 December 2017|work=HPCwire|date=June 8, 2017}}</ref><ref name="Touchstone">{{cite news |last1=Ahlberg Touchstone |first1=Liz |date=April 13, 2017 |title=Nanopores could map small changes in DNA that signal big shifts in cancer |url=https://phys.org/news/2017-04-nanopores-small-dna-big-shifts.html |access-date=28 December 2017 |work=Phys.Org}}</ref>

=== Early Work: Transport in Low-Dimensional Systems and Device Modeling (1980s–1990s) ===
Leburton first gained recognition in the early 1980s for his foundational contributions to transport phenomena in low-dimensional semiconductor systems.<ref name="Leburton1984">{{cite journal|last1=Leburton|first1=J. P.|title=Size effects on polar optical phonon scattering of 1-D and 2-D electron gas in synthetic semiconductors|journal=Journal of Applied Physics|date=15 November 1984|volume=56|issue=10|pages=2850–2855|doi=10.1063/1.333820|bibcode=1984JAP....56.2850L}}</ref>

His 1984 paper on optical phonon scattering in 1D and 2D structures (''[[Journal of Applied Physics]]'') was among the first to rigorously address dissipation at the [[nanoscale]], and is now considered a landmark study.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Size effects on polar optical phonon scattering of 1-D and 2-D electron gas in synthetic semiconductors |url=https://experts.illinois.edu/en/publications/size-effects-on-polar-optical-phonon-scattering-of-1-d-and-2-d-el/fingerprints/ |access-date=2025-09-03 |website=Illinois Experts |language=en}}</ref>

He later developed a multi-subband Monte Carlo simulation framework for quantum wires incorporating [[quantum]] confinement<ref name="Woo" /><ref name="Andoa">{{cite journal |last1=Andoa |first1=Yuji |last2=Cappy |first2=Alain |date=15 September 1993 |title=Ensemble Monte Carlo simulation for electron transport in quantum wire structures |url=https://users.soe.ucsc.edu/~tyamada/Course_handouts/Yamada-Sone/ref2.pdf |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |volume=74 |issue=6 |page=3983 |bibcode=1993JAP....74.3983A |doi=10.1063/1.354441 |access-date=27 December 2017}}</ref><ref name="Briggs">{{cite journal |last1=Briggs |first1=S. |last2=Leburton |first2=J. P. |date=15 October 1988 |title=Size effects in multisubband quantum wire structures |journal=Physical Review B |volume=38 |issue=12 |pages=8163–8170 |bibcode=1988PhRvB..38.8163B |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.38.8163 |pmid=9945568}}</ref> and hot-carrier effects in a self-consistent way.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Jovanovic |first1=D. |chapter=Monte Carlo Simulation of Quasi-One-Dimensional Systems |date=1991 |title=Monte Carlo Device Simulation |pages=191–218 |editor-last=Hess |editor-first=Karl |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4615-4026-7_7 |access-date=2025-09-03 |place=Boston, MA |publisher=Springer US |doi=10.1007/978-1-4615-4026-7_7 |isbn=978-1-4613-6800-7 |last2=Leburton |first2=J. P.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> This led to the prediction of [[Intersubband polariton|inter-subband]] optical phonon resonance, which was experimentally validated by K. Ismail at [[IBM]] in 1992.<ref name="Ismail">{{cite journal|last1=Jovanovic|first1=D|last2=Leburton|first2=J P|last3=Ismail|first3=K|title=Evidence of resonant intersubband optical phonon scattering in quantum wires|journal=Semiconductor Science and Technology|date=1 May 1994|volume=9|issue=5S|pages=882–885|doi=10.1088/0268-1242/9/5S/130|bibcode=1994SeScT...9..882J}}</ref><ref name="Jovanovic">{{cite journal |last1=Jovanovic |first1=D. |last2=Leburton |first2=J.P. |date=January 1992 |title=Electron-phonon interaction and velocity oscillations in quantum wire structures |journal=Superlattices and Microstructures |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=141–143 |bibcode=1992SuMi...11..141J |doi=10.1016/0749-6036(92)90238-Z}}</ref>

During the 1990s, Leburton's research expanded into non-linear transport and electro-thermal effects, long before "[[Thermal management (electronics)|thermal management]]" became a key issue in nanodevice design. His work showed how quantum confinement could modulate electron-phonon interactions, offering new pathways to control heat dissipation in electronic devices.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lack of thermoelectric effect is cool feature in carbon nanotubes – News Bureau |url=https://news.illinois.edu/lack-of-thermoelectric-effect-is-cool-feature-in-carbon-nanotubes/ |access-date=2025-09-03 |language=en-US}}</ref> This culminated in a 2005 ''[[Physical Review Letters]]'' paper that provided one of the first coherent electro-thermal models for carbon nanotubes, demonstrating excellent agreement with experiments.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kuroda |first1=Marcelo A. |last2=Cangellaris |first2=Andreas |last3=Leburton |first3=Jean-Pierre |date=2005-12-21 |title=Nonlinear Transport and Heat Dissipation in Metallic Carbon Nanotubes |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.266803 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=95 |issue=26 |article-number=266803 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.266803 |pmid=16486384 |arxiv=cond-mat/0507210 |bibcode=2005PhRvL..95z6803K }}</ref>

Concurrently, he made pivotal contributions to [[Optoelectronics|optoelectronic]] device physics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Advanced Optoelectronic Devices {{!}} Mohseni Research Group |url=https://bisol.northwestern.edu/advanced-optoelectronic-devices/ |access-date=2025-09-03 |website=bisol.northwestern.edu}}</ref> Working on layered semiconductor structures and superlattices, he developed the first multi-band pseudopotential model for calculating refractive indices, which supported impurity-induced layer disordering experiments by Nick Holonyak's group (''Physical Review B'', 1986).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-07-13 |title=Kaleidoscope: Phys. Rev. B 86, 045114 |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/kaleidoscope/prb/86/4/045114 |access-date=2025-09-03 |website=Physical Review B |language=en}}</ref>

He proposed novel designs for high-efficiency [[solar cells]] (''Applied Physics Letters'', 1986) and mid-infrared laser structures using asymmetric quantum wells,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kahen |first1=K. B. |last2=Leburton |first2=J. P. |date=1986-09-22 |title=Exciton effects in the index of refraction of multiple quantum wells and superlattices |journal=Applied Physics Letters |volume=49 |issue=12 |pages=734–736 |doi=10.1063/1.97583 |bibcode=1986ApPhL..49..734K |issn=0003-6951}}</ref><ref name="Hickernell">{{cite journal |last1=Hickernell |first1=Robert K. |last2=Christensen |first2=David H. |last3=Pellegrino |first3=Joseph G. |last4=Wang |first4=Jin |last5=Leburton |first5=Jean-Pierre |date=15 March 1994 |title=Determination of the complex refractive index of individual quantum wells from distributed reflectance |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |volume=75 |issue=6 |pages=3056–3059 |bibcode=1994JAP....75.3056H |doi=10.1063/1.356153}}</ref> including collaborative work with the [[University of Paris]] (''Electronics Letters'', 1995).

He also addressed slow carrier dynamics in modulation-doped quantum wells using Monte Carlo simulations (''PRB'', 1991) and helped develop the BRAQWETT nonlinear optical modulator in collaboration with Bell Labs (''JAP'', 1993).<ref name="Matagne">{{cite journal|last1=Leburton|first1=Jean-Pierre|last2=Nagaraja|first2=Satyadev|last3=Matagne|first3=Philippe|last4=Martin|first4=Richard M.|title=Spintronics and exchange engineering in coupled quantum dots|journal=Microelectronics Journal|date=May 2003|volume=34|issue=5–8|pages=485–489|doi=10.1016/S0026-2692(03)00080-6|url=https://experts.illinois.edu/en/publications/spintronics-and-exchange-engineering-in-coupled-quantum-dots|access-date=29 December 2017|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="Woo" /> In 2009, Leburton developed the first theory of the high frequency response and limitations of the light emitting transistor invented by his colleagues at the [[University of Illinois]], while providing design guidelines to improve the device performance a few years later.<ref name="Ivchenko">{{cite book |last1=Ivchenko |first1=Eougenious L. |title=Superlattices and Other Heterostructures Symmetry and Optical Phenomena |last2=Pikus |first2=Grigory |date=1995 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-642-97589-9 |location=Berlin, Heidelberg}}</ref><ref name="Hess">{{cite journal |last1=Leburton |first1=J. P. |last2=Hess |first2=K. |last3=Holonyak |first3=N. |last4=Coleman |first4=J. J. |last5=Camras |first5=M. |date=July 1983 |title=Index of refraction of AlAs-GaAs superlattices |url=https://experts.illinois.edu/en/publications/index-of-refraction-of-alas-gaas-superlattices |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |volume=54 |issue=7 |pages=4230–4231 |bibcode=1983JAP....54.4230L |doi=10.1063/1.332526 |url-access=subscription |access-date=27 December 2017}}</ref><ref name="Kahen">{{cite journal |last1=Kahen |first1=K. B. |last2=Leburton |first2=J. P. |date=15 April 1986 |title=Optical constants of GaAs-As superlattices and multiple quantum wells |journal=Physical Review B |volume=33 |issue=8 |pages=5465–5472 |bibcode=1986PhRvB..33.5465K |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.33.5465 |pmid=9939051}}</ref>

=== Tunneling Devices and Negative Differential Resistance (Mid 1980s–2000s) ===
In the mid 1980, among six different interpretations of a puzzling oscillatory behavior uncovered by [[IBM]] in the electronic current across a semiconductor tunneling hetero-junction, Leburton provided the first coherent explanation based on a space-charge effect feedback to the tunnel barrier.<ref>{{Cite book |date=1987 |editor-last=Devreese |editor-first=J. T. |editor2-last=Peeters |editor2-first=F. M. |title=The Physics of the Two-Dimensional Electron Gas |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4613-1907-8 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-1907-8 |isbn=978-1-4612-9061-2 }}</ref>

Then, by the late 1980s, Leburton was exploring tunneling injection mechanisms in field-effect transistors to induce [[negative differential resistance]] (NDR), an effect useful in high-speed electronics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Leburton |first1=J. P. |last2=Kolodzey |first2=J. |last3=Briggs |first3=S. |date=1988 |title=Bipolar tunneling field-effect transistor: A three-terminal negative differential resistance device for high-speed applications |url=http://www.scopus.com/inward/record.url?scp=36549104654&partnerID=8YFLogxK |journal=Applied Physics Letters |volume=52 |issue=19 |pages=1608–1610 |doi=10.1063/1.99056 |bibcode=1988ApPhL..52.1608L |issn=0003-6951}}</ref>

In 1991, he was awarded a U.S. patent for a three-terminal interband tunneling transistor, anticipating modern approaches to low-power MOSFET design.<ref>{{Cite patent|number=US5059545A|title=Three terminal tunneling device and method|gdate=1991-10-22|invent1=Frensley|invent2=Reed|inventor1-first=William R.|inventor2-first=Mark A.|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5059545A/en}}</ref>

In the early 1990s, he introduced the concept of '''"'''tunneling real-space transfer'''"''' in unipolar dual-channel FETs. This effect enabled abrupt gate-controlled NDR behavior, first demonstrated experimentally in 1992 (''IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices'').<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bigelow |first1=J. M. |last2=Leburton |first2=J. P. |date=1990-08-20 |title=Tunneling real-space transfer induced by wave function hybridization in modulation-doped heterostructures |journal=Applied Physics Letters |volume=57 |issue=8 |pages=795–797 |doi=10.1063/1.103423 |bibcode=1990ApPhL..57..795B |issn=0003-6951}}</ref>

Very recently, he modified the design of a three-terminal quantum cascade laser proposed by J. Dallesasse to discover a new kind of ultra-sensitive electro-optic bistabilities in the resonant tunneling superlattice transistor.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=Zhiyuan |last2=Chen |first2=Kanuo |last3=Hsiao |first3=Fu-Chen |last4=Wang |first4=Zhuoran |last5=Dallesasse |first5=John M. |last6=Leburton |first6=Jean-Pierre |date=2017-12-15 |title=Modeling of the electrically-tunable transistor-injected quantum cascade laser |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |volume=122 |issue=23 |page=235701 |doi=10.1063/1.4999751 |issn=0021-8979}}</ref><ref name="Wang">{{cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Yue|last2=Yang|first2=Qiuping|last3=Wang|first3=Zhimin|title=The evolution of nanopore sequencing|journal=Frontiers in Genetics|date=7 January 2015|volume=5|page=449|doi=10.3389/fgene.2014.00449|pmid=25610451|pmc=4285804|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="NHGRI">{{cite web|title=Advanced Sequencing Technology Awards 2005|url=https://www.genome.gov/15015202/advanced-sequencing-technology-awards-2005/|website=National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI)|access-date=28 December 2017}}</ref>

=== Semiconductor Bio-Nanoelectronics and Solid-State Nanopores (2006–Present) ===
In the mid-2000s, Leburton transitioned to the interface of [[semiconductor physics]] and [[biotechnology]], recognizing the potential of solid-state nanostructures for [[biosensing]] and [[Diagnosis|diagnostics]].<ref name="Beckman2006">{{cite web |title=Developing Semiconductor Membranes for Bio-molecule Control in Nanopores |url=https://beckman.illinois.edu/content/uploads/files/annual-reports/annual-report-2006-2007.pdf |access-date=28 December 2017 |website=Beckman Institute Annual Report 2006-2007 |page=20}}</ref> In 2006, he proposed the concept of an ionic field-effect transistor (iFET) using semiconductor membranes with p/n junction doping to modulate ionic currents (''Nanotechnology'', 2006).<ref name="Kloeppel">{{cite news |last1=Kloeppel |first1=James E. |date=July 12, 2007 |title=Semiconductor membrane mimics biological behavior of ion channels |url=https://news.illinois.edu/view/6367/206600 |access-date=29 December 2017 |work=Illinois News Bureau}}</ref> This work was patented and later licensed by Oxford Nanopore Technologies (''U.S. Patent 8,192,600 B2'', 2012). His team was also a finalist for the Best Paper Award at the 2007 IEEE Nanotechnology Conference.<ref name="McGaughey" />

In 2013, Leburton introduced a paradigm-shifting idea of using [[graphene]] membranes<ref name="Dambrot">{{cite news |last1=Dambrot |first1=Stuart Mason |date=October 30, 2013 |title=Through a nanopore, ionically: Graphene quantum transistor for next-generation DNA sensing |url=https://phys.org/news/2013-10-nanopore-ionically-graphene-quantum-transistor.html |access-date=28 December 2017 |work=Phys.org}}</ref> with nanopores for DNA sequencing, utilizing graphene's atomic thinness and tunable conductivity to enhance resolution and signal-to-noise ratio (''PNAS'', 2013).<ref name="Cuffari">{{cite news |last1=Cuffari |first1=Benedette |date=April 4, 2017 |title=Nanotechnology in 2017: The Story So Far January - May |url=https://www.azonano.com/article.aspx?ArticleID=4443 |access-date=28 December 2017 |work=AZONANO}}</ref><ref name="Qiu">{{cite journal |last1=Qiu |first1=Hu |last2=Sarathy |first2=Aditya |last3=Schulten |first3=Klaus |last4=Leburton |first4=Jean-Pierre |date=11 April 2017 |title=Detection and mapping of DNA methylation with 2D material nanopores |journal=npj 2D Materials and Applications |volume=1 |issue=1 |article-number=3 |doi=10.1038/s41699-017-0005-7 |doi-access=free|pmc=5794036 |pmid=29399640}}</ref>

More recently, his group extended this approach to other [[Single-layer materials|2D materials]] like [[Molybdenum disulfide|MoS₂]] for ultra-sensitive molecular detection, offering applications in drug delivery, biomarker sensing, and in-vivo diagnostics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Athreya |first1=Nagendra Bala Murali |last2=Sarathy |first2=Aditya |last3=Leburton |first3=Jean-Pierre |date=2018-05-25 |title=Large Scale Parallel DNA Detection by Two-Dimensional Solid-State Multipore Systems |journal=ACS Sensors |volume=3 |issue=5 |pages=1032–1039 |doi=10.1021/acssensors.8b00192 |pmid=29663800 |bibcode=2018ACSSe...3.1032A }}</ref>

Very recently, his interest in [[Nanofluidics|nano-fluidics]] led him to the discovery of a new coulomb drag effect in electrolytic nanoscale channels, where the ion flow induces a drag of the free electronic charge resulting in a significant electric current amplification in the surrounding conductor .<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Xiong |first1=Mingye |last2=Song |first2=Kewei |last3=Leburton |first3=Jean-Pierre |date=December 2023 |title=Ionic coulomb drag in nanofluidic semiconductor channels for energy harvest |journal=Nano Energy |volume=117 |article-number=108860 |doi=10.1016/j.nanoen.2023.108860 |bibcode=2023NEne..11708860X |issn=2211-2855}}</ref> This effect that has broad range of applications in non-fossil fuel generation was rapidly confirmed with the use of carbon nanotubes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jiang |first1=Yisha |last2=Liu |first2=Wenchao |last3=Wang |first3=Tao |last4=Wu |first4=Yitian |last5=Mei |first5=Tingting |last6=Wang |first6=Li |last7=Xu |first7=Guoheng |last8=Wang |first8=Yude |last9=Liu |first9=Nannan |last10=Xiao |first10=Kai |date=2024-10-03 |title=A nanofluidic chemoelectrical generator with enhanced energy harvesting by ion-electron Coulomb drag |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=15 |issue=1 |page=8582 |doi=10.1038/s41467-024-52892-4  |doi-access=free|pmid=39362886 |pmc=11449912 |bibcode=2024NatCo..15.8582J |issn=2041-1723}}</ref>

=== Recent Advances in Wide-Bandgap Semiconductors and High-Power Electronics (2020s) ===
In his most recent work, Leburton has focused on wide-bandgap [[semiconductors]], particularly diamond and cubic GaN (c-GaN), for applications in green LEDs, high-frequency transistors, and power electronics.<ref name="Wide Bandgap Semiconductors 2024">{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Jaekwon |last2=Bayram |first2=Can |last3=Leburton |first3=Jean-Pierre |date=September 2024 |title=High Field Transport in (Ultra) Wide Bandgap Semiconductors: Diamond Versus Cubic GaN |journal=IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices |volume=71 |issue=9 |pages=5638–5644 |doi=10.1109/TED.2024.3421182 |bibcode=2024ITED...71.5638L |issn=1557-9646|doi-access=free }}</ref> In a 2023 study with Jaekwon Lee and Can Bayram, he investigated high-field transport dynamics in these materials, showing how non-randomizing polar optical phonon (POP) scattering in c-GaN enables [[electron cooling]], resulting in higher peak drift velocities compared to diamond.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Jaekwon |last2=Leburton |first2=Jean-Pierre |last3=Bayram |first3=Can |date=2023-05-01 |title=Design tradeoffs between traditional hexagonal and emerging cubic InXGa(1X)N/GaN-based green light-emitting diodes |url=https://opg.optica.org/josab/abstract.cfm?uri=josab-40-5-1017 |journal=JOSA B |language=EN |volume=40 |issue=5 |pages=1017–1023 |doi=10.1364/JOSAB.483832 |bibcode=2023JOSAB..40.1017L |osti=1970117 |issn=1520-8540}}</ref>

He also co-authored of a new software for the simulation and optimization of wide [[Band gap|band-gap]] [[Cubic nitre|cubic nitride]] QW devices  which is auspicious of its future utilizations in  high-efficiency droop green and blue LEDs. These findings provide new insight into material behavior under extreme conditions and inform the design of next-generation optoelectronic devices.<ref name="Wide Bandgap Semiconductors 2024"/>

== Recognition ==
Across his career, Leburton has developed full-band Monte Carlo transport models, multi-subband simulations, and quantum many-body frameworks that have shaped our understanding of quantum transport, carrier mobility, and device scaling.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Fischetti |first1=M. V. |chapter=Monte Carlo Simulation of High-Energy Electron Transport in Silicon: Is There a Short-Cut to Happiness? |date=1996 |title=Hot Carriers in Semiconductors |pages=475–480 |editor-last=Hess |editor-first=Karl |place=Boston, MA |publisher=Springer US |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-0401-2_109 |isbn=978-1-4613-0401-2 |last2=Laux |first2=S. E. |last3=Crabbé |first3=E. |editor2-last=Leburton |editor2-first=Jean-Pierre |editor3-last=Ravaioli |editor3-first=Umberto}}</ref> He has also contributed theoretical models for quantum fountain lasers, quantum cascade lasers, and vertical tunneling FETs, collaborating with leading institutions in the US, Canada, Brazil, Europe, and Asia.<ref name="Illinois" />

In 2025, Jean‑Pierre Leburton was named a Fellow of the [[National Academy of Inventors]] (NAI), recognizing his distinguished contributions to nanotechnology and semiconductor research. He was among 169 U.S. and 16 international inventors selected to the 2025 class of NAI Fellows a group honored for their innovation and impact in translating research into patented technologies that benefit society, and he will be formally inducted at the NAI's annual conference in June 2026 in Los Angeles.<ref name=":2" />
